query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A short sub-eutectic annealing treatment at approximately 700 °C for 2–5 hours will partially stabilize the dual-phase lamellar interfaces in the eutectic HEA by relieving residual stresses and inducing nanoscale precipitates. This treatment reduces dislocation pile-ups and local stress concentrations, thereby enhancing room-temperature tensile ductility and slightly increasing yield strength relative to the as-cast alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies prone to dislocation pile-up and local stress concentrations during room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Short sub-eutectic annealing treatment at approximately 700 °C for 2–5 hours.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing (strain rate ~10⁻³ s⁻¹) with the potential to extend evaluation to mildly elevated temperatures to observe thermal stability.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined interphase boundaries with finely dispersed nanoscale precipitates induced by the annealing treatment that relieve residual stresses.
generation.mechanism: The controlled annealing relieves localized residual stresses at the dual-phase boundaries and promotes the formation of fine, coherent precipitates. This treatment mitigates dislocation pile-up at these interfaces, reducing local stress concentrations that can trigger microcracking, thereby enhancing ductility while maintaining or slightly increasing strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: An expected increase in yield strength by approximately 10–15% (e.g., from ~900 MPa to ~1000–1050 MPa) and an improvement in tensile ductility from around 10% to 15–20% elongation at room temperature.
generation.baseline: The untreated, as-cast eutectic HEA, which exhibits limited room-temperature ductility (~10% elongation) and tensile yield strength of around 900 MPa.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under controlled, uniform thermal treatment conditions; deviations in temperature or time may lead to excessive coarsening or phase instability that could negate the intended improvements. The improvements are expected under standard room-temperature tensile testing conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of ductility and strength improvement is sensitive to exact annealing parameters and the starting microstructure. There is also uncertainty regarding the long-term thermal stability of the modified interfaces.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the eutectic HEA: one set undergoes the proposed sub-eutectic annealing treatment (700 °C for 2–5 hours) and the other remains in the as-cast state. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests (strain rate ~10⁻³ s⁻¹) and perform TEM analysis to assess dislocation behavior and precipitate formation at the phase boundaries.
measurements: Yield strength and percent elongation from tensile testing
TEM/HAADF-STEM imaging to observe dislocation pile-up and precipitate distribution along the phase boundaries
Microhardness measurements to assess local mechanical properties
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in dislocation pile-ups or local interface stress concentrations, and if the tensile yield strength does not increase by ~10–15% while ductility does not improve from ~10% to at least 15%, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] . decision.trend: Early work on eutectic high-entropy alloys with lamellar fcc/B2 microstructures (PMC4145285) has shown excellent strength and moderate ductility but also suggested that local strain concentrations at phase boundaries could lead to crack initiation under tension. Subsequent studies on similarly brittle B2-containing high-entropy or refractory high-entropy alloys (PMC5995863) demonstrated that multistage thermal processing to modify or refine these lamellar or precipitated interfaces can significantly enhance ductility while preserving or improving strength. Nevertheless, an approach that specifically targets dislocation pile-ups at interphase boundaries—without altering the overall composition—remains an open challenge.
decision.unsolved: Despite improved processing routes for producing dual-phase eutectic HEAs, the persistent issue of dislocation pile-ups at phase boundaries remains. These pile-ups can trigger local stress concentrations and microcracking in the brittle lamellar constituents during room-temperature deformation. A single, well-controlled heat-treatment or thermomechanical path that relieves boundary stress concentrations and refines boundary structures, yet avoids excessive or inhomogeneous coarsening, is still lacking.
decision.lever: A short sub-eutectic annealing (e.g., ~700 °C for 2–5 hours) of the as-cast lamellar colonies to induce partial interface stabilization and nanoscale precipitation without changing the overall composition
decision.why: Building on insights from prior EHEA studies (PMC4145285) and analogous B2-containing systems (PMC5995863), a controlled annealing step just below the eutectic temperature will reduce dislocation pile-ups by (1) relieving residual stress at the dual-phase lamellar boundaries and (2) inducing fine precipitates that stabilize interfaces. This can mitigate local stress concentrations, improving ductility while retaining or slightly enhancing strength. Based on prior evidence, we predict an increase in yield strength up to ~10–15% over the untreated alloy (e.g., from ~900 MPa to ~1000–1050 MPa) and a corresponding increase in tensile ductility from ~10% to ~15–20% elongation at room temperature. Tensile testing at a strain rate of ~10⁻³ s⁻¹ from ambient to moderately elevated temperatures will validate these improvements. A falsification experiment can be conducted by omitting the sub-eutectic annealing step in a control batch and comparing the resulting microstructure, dislocation behavior, and ductility to confirm that the observed improvements originate from the proposed interface modifications.
